newsitem.title: USA: N.J. board submits final power deregulation plan.
newsitem.headline: N.J. board submits final power deregulation plan.

text.p: New Jersey's Board of Public Utilties submitted its final recommendations in a plan aimed at fully deregulating the state's electricity industry and lowering electricity rates, the board said Wednesday.
The plan calls for electricity rate cuts of five to 10 percent from October, 1998, and allowing all New Jerseyans to choose their electricity supplier by July 2000.
It will now be sent to the governor and state legislature for approval.
The Board, in a statement, said the proposal moved the target date for full retail choice ahead by nine months from its earlier proposal.
"Further, the Board clarified that the rate reductions would not be offset by charges that would be paid by utility customers to recover stranded costs," the statement said.

Stranded costs are those costs incurred by utilities for power plants, transmission lines and other assets built in the days of a regulated industry, when they were allowed to recover these costs through higher prices to consumers.
"Since stranded costs are currently included in rates, no rate increase is required to allow for their recovery," the board said.
Though stranded costs are roughly estimated to be in the billions of dollars for public utilities operating in New Jersey, no firm numbers yet exist.
"We are giving utilities the opportunity to recover stranded costs, but we are not guaranteeing recovery," said board president Herbert Tate.
"The Board does not want a one-size-fits-all percentage of recovery for all utilities. Instead, we want to address stranded costs on a utility-by-utility basis."
He said each utility must present the board with their own proposal for lowering costs to consumers.
"They must show us that they have done everything possible to reduce stranded costs before we will consider allowing them to recover any of them." he said in a statement.

The plan also calls for consumer and environmental safeguards to ensure universal power service, prevent consumer fraud, and fight a rise in air pollution by requiring power suppliers to disclose emissions levels from their plants.
According to the plan, retail competition will be phased in from October, 1998, for 10 percent of the state's residential, commercial and industrial customers, double the board's earlier proposal.
Citing a planned energy tax cut, the board said New Jersey power prices will actually drop 10 to 15 percent from current rates, which are about 50 percent above the national average.
But details of the tax cut or a timeframe in which such savings were likely to be realized were not given.
Three models for implementing competition were evaluated.
The poolco model would allow local utilities to buy the cheapest power from a power pool on behalf of its customers.
The direct access model would allow customers to go directly to suppliers to negotiate the price of their power.

"The third option, and the one proposed by the Board, is a hybrid of the first two. Customers can choose to buy electricity either from the pool through their local utility or directly from another supplier," the board said.
Other aspects of the plan call for unbundling, or breaking into separate billings, the cost of power generation, transmission, distribution, and related services.
New Jersey Governor Christine Whitman, commenting on the plan, said it "would bring energy costs in line with those of competing states so that we may remain 'Open for Business'."

Neighboring Pennsylvania last November approved a similar plan to lower power rates to industrial, commercial, and eventually residential customers through open competition in its electricity industry.
Public Service Electric and Gas Co (PSE&G), a subsidiary of Public Service Enterprise Group Inc and one of the state's biggest utilities, called the final proposal a "fair and flexible plan."
PSE&G's president and chief operating officer, Lawrence Codey, said the company would be prepared to file its deregulation proposal in July.
((--James Jelter, New York Power Desk 212 859 1621))
